stimuli.title: Seven people live on different floors of a seven-storey building. Floor 1 is the bottom floor, and floor 7 is the top floor.
stimuli.body:
Clues:
1. Zara is exactly 3 positions above Nisha.
2. In the stated ordering, Nikhil comes before Yash, and Yash comes before Farhan.
3. Nikhil is at floor 4.
4. Uma is exactly 2 positions above Lakshya.
stimuli.solution: floor 1: Lakshya; floor 2: Nisha; floor 3: Uma; floor 4: Nikhil; floor 5: Zara; floor 6: Yash; floor 7: Farhan

stimuli.title: Seven labelled boxes are stacked vertically, with one box in each position.

stimuli.title: Seven people have interviews in seven consecutive months from January to July, one per month.
stimuli.body:

2. Firoz is immediately later than Lakshya.

stimuli.solution: January: Yuvraj; February: Varun; March: Priya; April: Lakshya; May: Firoz; June: Kavya; July: Rohan

stimuli.title: Seven employees hold seven distinct ranks (rank 1 is junior-most and rank 7 is senior-most).
stimuli.body:
Clues:
1. Tanvi is exactly 3 positions senior to Yash.
2. Harish is at rank 1.
3. Jai is immediately senior to Chitra.
4. There are exactly 2 positions between Uday and Chitra.
5. There are exactly 1 positions between Jai and Harish.

stimuli.title: In a certain coded language, each word has one unique code.
stimuli.body:
thunder honest yellow = fa mu no
breeze summit yellow = no li ju
thunder summit basket = li mu qa
breeze honest basket = fa qa ju
stimuli.solution: yellow=no, thunder=mu, honest=fa, summit=li, breeze=ju, basket=qa

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain X < Z < Q > U < W, decide which conclusions follow. I: Z ≥ W. II: Q = W.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is not necessarily true and II is not necessarily true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain V < Z < Q ≥ U ≤ W, decide which conclusions follow. I: U ≤ W. II: Z > U.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is always true and II is not necessarily true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain Z ≤ X > U ≤ Q ≤ V, decide which conclusions follow. I: Q ≤ V. II: U ≤ Q.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is always true and II is always true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain P < V < Z < U = R, decide which conclusions follow. I: P ≥ U. II: Z < U.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is not necessarily true and II is always true.

questions.stem: Given the inequality chain U > S ≤ Z ≥ X ≤ P, decide which conclusions follow. I: U ≥ S. II: U ≥ P.
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: Exhaustive valid-order checking confirms: I is always true and II is not necessarily true.

questions.stem: Statements: All readers are pilots. No pilots are workers. Conclusions: I. No readers are workers. II. Some readers are workers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: A is contained in B, while B and C are disjoint.

questions.stem: Statements: Some bakers are farmers. No farmers are singers. Conclusions: I. Some bakers are not singers. II. All bakers are singers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: The A∩B members cannot be C.

questions.stem: Statements: Some teachers are runners. Some runners are readers. Conclusions: I. Some teachers are readers. II. Some runners are teachers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: The two Some overlaps need not coincide; Some A are B converts to Some B are A.

questions.stem: Statements: All poets are runners. Some bakers are poets. Conclusions: I. Some bakers are runners. II. Some runners are bakers. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: The existing C∩A members must lie in B, proving both conclusions.

questions.stem: Statements: No poets are readers. All coders are readers. Some coders are readers. Conclusions: I. No poets are coders. II. Some coders are not poets. Which conclusion follows?
options: Both conclusions I and II follow
Either conclusion I or II follows
questions.explanation: All C members belong to B, disjoint from A; some C are explicitly given.

questions.stem: Ritu walks 15 km north, then 12 km east, then 3 km south and finally 3 km west. What is her shortest distance from the starting point?
questions.explanation: Net north = 12 km and east = 9 km. Distance = √(12²+9²) = 15 km.

questions.stem: Kiran moves 3 km north, 18 km east, 9 km south and 3 km west. In which direction is Kiran from the start?

questions.stem: A cyclist travels 27 km north, 12 km east, 15 km south and 3 km west. What total distance did the cyclist travel?
questions.explanation: Total path length = 27+12+15+3=57 km (not displacement).

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 17x + 72 = 0. Equation II: y² + 9y + 20 = 0. Which option is always correct?
questions.explanation: Roots of x are -9 and -8; roots of y are -5 and -4. Hence x < y.

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 12x + 35 = 0. Equation II: y² + 7y + 10 = 0. Which option is always correct?

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 11x + 18 = 0. Equation II: y² + 11y + 28 = 0. Which option is always correct?

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 5x + 6 = 0. Equation II: y² + 15y + 56 = 0. Which option is always correct?

questions.stem: Compare x and y. Equation I: x² + 7x + 10 = 0. Equation II: y² + 12y + 35 = 0. Which option is always correct?
